subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret that I was unable to communicate with the Prime Minister in this regard; I had no information on the matter until we arrived back here a few minutes ago. Has the Prime Minister anything to say regarding the coup in Ghana involving the overthrow of the Nkrumah administration; and what is the position in that country of the 100 or so Canadians who usually live there?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my right hon. friend knows I have had only a few moments to look at the overnight telegrams, but I did examine this particular one. While it is not definitive, in that there may have been developments since this message was sent, it did indicate that there was a military coup early in the morning; that there was some firing which went on for a comparatively short time, then Accra became calm.
What will be the further course of the move against the government, of course, I do not know at the present time. It seems to have been a military revolt against the existing government. The disturbances have been short and were reduced to a minimum, according to the message I received.
With regard to the position of the Canadians in Accra, we are told that at the present time there is no cause for anxiety. There are a good many Canadians there, but the information I have at the moment indicates that they were not in any danger of any kind. I will be glad to keep the house and my right hon. friend informed of events as they occur.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: I know the Prime Minister did not have time to look into this matter, Mr. Speaker, but at the same time I should like to ask a question which I think is uppermost in the minds of many Canadians, and it is this. What is the basis upon which recognition is granted of an insurgent group that takes over government in this way? What length of time is usually allowed to elapse before a government ceases to exist diplomatically, and recognition is given to an incoming government? Is this insurrection and the ousting of the Nkrumah government of such a nature that early recognition may be expected?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy or wise to be dogmatic in regard to the conditions which warrant recognition after a government has been overthrown. It depends, of course, on circumstances. Sometimes the new government is given recognition very quickly, as in the case of Nigeria a few weeks ago. At other times we have waited. A most important consideration is whether the new regime seems to be in control of the country, a control which is at least tacitly admitted by the country's people in so far as this can be ascertained.
Another consideration is that we should get in touch at once with our friends, and especially with our friends in the commonwealth, to see if they have information that we have not got. Very often we act in concert in these matters.
I do not think I can add anything more at the present time, Mr. Speaker. There have
February 24, 1966

Inquiries of the Ministry been occasions, and I think that the instance of Nigeria was one of these occasions, when we in this country gave no formal recognition but just carried on under the assumption that there had been a change of government, there might not be the kind of revolution which required formal recognition.
I am not sure whether that is the situation which will apply to Ghana. In the Nigerian situation we acted in concert with other commonwealth governments, which took the same attitude we did, that no formal recognition of the new regime was required.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: That was the reason for the question. I wondered whether a new rule had evolved within the commonwealth by which, where an insurrection takes place and a change of government results, the course is no longer followed of recognizing the new regime but rather of regarding it merely as a continuation of the one that was in power at the time of the overthrow.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Such a development, Mr. Speaker, might become a kind of normal attitude inside the commonwealth. It has not always been the case. I think in respect of Zanzibar there was formal recognition of the change. Whether that applies to Ghana I cannot say, because I think it is too soon after the event to know exactly what will happen.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

Secretary of State for External Affairs and ask if there is any word about the situation in Uganda that might clear up rumours we have heard, and that might also clear up rumours relating to the well-being of Canadian citizens there.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister has indicated the word we have received from our high commissioner is that according to present reports the safety of Canadians is not in question.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Uganda. The question was about Uganda.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker. I thought the question was about the safety of Canadians-

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: In Uganda, about which rumours are rampant today.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: That is a country in Africa.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the wise course would be to wait and see whether those rumours have any foundation in fact.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the country of Ghana on the west coast of Africa. Would the minister inform us how many Canadian service personnel are in that country for the purpose of training the Ghanaian army, and whether or not these men might now be recalled?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: There are 19 personnel there; three R.C.A.F. officers, 14 army officers and two N.C.O.'s, who assist in a training program. In the formal agreement between Canada and Ghana which defines the functions of the team it is stipulated that the members of the team will in no circumstances, of course, become involved in operational roles of a police or military nature. We shall have to consider in the light of events whether or not they should be recalled.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence. In view of the situation now existing in Ghana have any fresh instructions been sent to the Canadian military personnel there, in particular as to whether they are to continue their normal training activities with the Ghanaian armed forces; or have they been instructed to suspend this in the meantime?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minisier of National Defence):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been no change in the instructions they have received.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question I should like to direct to the Minister of National Defence which is consequent upon the answer he gave to a question I asked a moment ago. Does he not think that it would be desirable to send instructions to the Canadian military personnel in Ghana to suspend their ordinary training duties in association with the Ghanaian forces until the present situation has cleared itself?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: GHANA-REPORTED OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENT BY MILITARY FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we should first find out what the facts are. As soon as we have received a report this will be discussed with the Department of External Affairs, which really is responsible for financing these training operations in countries other than NATO countries.

subtopic: U.S. CUSTOMS REGULATIONS RESPECTING BOX CARS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: U.S. CUSTOMS REGULATIONS RESPECTING BOX CARS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport and ask him whether there have been any recent changes in United States customs regulations which would further aggravate the present disparity between the large numbers of Canadian box cars in the United States compared with the numbers of United States box cars in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: U.S. CUSTOMS REGULATIONS RESPECTING BOX CARS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman was good enough to give me notice of this question. Early last week I learned that the United States customs had approved the suspension until March 1 of normal customs duty requirements in the use of Canadian box cars for the handling of paper products originated by two shippers at Plattsburg, New York. I took immediate steps to draw the unfavourable aspects of this matter to the attention of the United States authorities, and I am very glad to say that this arrangement operated for only one day. I could give a more detailed answer, but I think that that perhaps might suffice.

subtopic: U.S. CUSTOMS REGULATIONS RESPECTING BOX CARS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the minister whether any representations are being made to the government of the United States to rectify the great disparity between the numbers of Canadian box cars in the United States and the numbers of United States box cars in Canada, which disparity for some time has been running at a ratio of almost three to one against Canada.

subtopic: U.S. CUSTOMS REGULATIONS RESPECTING BOX CARS
speechtext: Of course, Mr. Speaker, the United States railways are not under the direct control of the United States government. I understand that constant conversations are going on about this between the Association of American Railroads, as I think they are called over there, and our railways. I may say that the American Association of Railroads itself took action against this suspension, which was applied for by one railroad in the United States.

I think that the minister made an investigation; I have not had the opportunity since then to ask him if he had any information to give us, but I would like to know if it is true that one of the two individuals with Dr. Marcoux in a restaurant was a former executive secretary of a former Conservative minister-it would be a former minister of justice-who would have had in his possession a card identifying him as a member of the R.C.M.P., although not a member of the R.C.M.P., and who would have used that card to get statements from a restaurant owner in Montreal, under false representations?
That is an answer I would like to get from the minister. Did he make an investigation in that case? Is it true that two individuals pretended to be members of the R.C.M.P., whereas they had no right to do that, since they were not members of the R.C.M.P.?
Second, was Dr. Marcoux present when those individuals appeared? We suspect that he was present. At that time, was he party to those false representations?

I wish to thank the hon. member for Peace River and I hope that I am not being rude in asking for the floor. Yesterday, of course, we had two statements. We had a statement from the Minister of Justice and then we had a statement from the Prime Minister. I dealt yesterday particularly with the statement made by the Prime Minister. It did seem rather unusual that at the opening of discussion on these estimates we would have two statements, one from the Minister of Justice and one from the Prime Minister, and particularly that the Prime Minister should make a statement on these estimates.
We have dealt at some length with the Spencer case and I should now like to make a few general remarks with reference to the estimates. The first question has been answered with reference to the division of the department. We accept this fact but it has been somewhat difficult to determine who has jurisdiction over what. It does seem that under the present administration there has been, as I have already made reference, some divisive confusion about jurisdiction within the Department of Justice. I would hope that the minister will make a clear statement in that regard.
I would also say this. I wonder whether these hon. gentlemen have ever considered, since they feel there has to be legislation passed in order to set up the divisions, whether they really have the jurisdiction over certain matters which they claim to have. We would like to hear from the ministers, whether it be the Minister of Justice or the President of the Privy Council, under whose jurisdiction the administration of federal offences falls. I assume it would be the Minister of Justice. We should like to know also under whose jurisdiction the following items fall: National Parole Board, bankruptcy-I am going to have something to say about that in a few minutes-penitentiaries, the committee report on juvenile delinquency as well as the whole question of young offenders, and the Combines Investigation Act.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
No one would underestimate the importance of the administration of justice. After all, the tentacles of justice must stretch into all federal departments to obtain good, sound, honest government with equitable administration.
Co-ordination has always been the important thing so far as I am concerned in the administration of justice. What we have in

this administration, I repeat, is no co-ordination at all. What we have is divisive confusion. We on this side of the house do not know, parliament does not know, I do not think the government knows, nor do the people of Canada know, who is really Minister of Justice. As I say, there is divisive confusion. I have come to the conclusion that the Prime Minister, and I say this with respect, has run out of talent and is somewhat concerned, when he assigns a certain portfolio to a minister, whether he has confidence in him.
I used an illustration yesterday which I am going to use today, namely, the Canadian Wheat Board. This is an analogy which I shall come back to in so far as the Department of Justice is concerned. For years the Canadian Wheat Board was under the jurisdiction either of the Minister of Agriculture or of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. When the Prime Minister had to look for a new Minister of Agriculture and when he appointed a new Minister of Trade and Commerce he must have looked at both of them and said to himself: Neither of you has any administrative ability so far as the Wheat Board is concerned so I will leave that with the new Minister of Finance because he is the only man who seems to know anything about it.
Exactly the same sort of thing has happened with the Department of Justice. The Prime Minister probably said to himself: The Minister of Justice is a fine fellow but I do not know whether he can handle this or that phase. As a result, Mr. Chairman, we have divisive confusion and we cannot get any answers at all.
Yesterday I asked a question-this is an example of divisive confusion and it is why the Speaker and I seem to be at odds-which was ruled out of order by the Speaker. I knew I would be in difficulty when I asked another question today. But if there is a matter of importance in the nation today it is the question of crime, crime in high places and crime in other places. Its tentacles are creeping all through our society. I have heard the leader of our party and the hon. member for Yukon both say on many occasions something with which I am in full accord, that we should have an investigaton into crime in this nation. A royal commission should be set up.
We have just heard the hon. member for Lapointe talk about the Marcoux investigation. During the election Dr. Marcoux alleged that six members of the Creditistes had said

Of course not; he makes his speech and leaves. Well, I am not going to get into any argument; I am going to deal with the facts. What I was coming to, Mr. Chairman, was that certain charges were made by a former member of the House of Commons either during or before the last election. You will remember that parliament was dissolved because of an election, one which we did not call. I was always of the opinion that the reason parliament was dissolved was that the government were afraid to debate the report of the Dorion Commission. They called an election so they could sweep that under the carpet.
If I may return to the Marcoux matter, Mr. Chairman, Dr. Marcoux made some serious charges. He also made a serious charge against one of your own colleagues sitting on the front bench. But what did the Minister of Justice say? After all, he is Minister of Justice for the government. I am not saying that the decision he took was his personal decision; what I say is that it was the government's decision. I am also not making any personal attack on the minister. I know that he once made the same sort of attack on our leader but I am not going to attack him. Let me make it clear that I am attacking the administration of this department by the government.
When this matter was brought before the Minister of Justice he said that it was not a federal matter and swept it under the carpet. Surely when serious charges of bribery are made against members of parliament it is a matter for the federal government and the House of Commons.
Supply-Justice
Therefore I ask at the outset, what respect can the Canadian people or parliament have today for the administration of justice under a government which sweeps things like the Dr. Marcoux scandal under the carpet and which calls an election so that the matter cannot be debated? This affair is now a thing of the past. The government has also prevented debate on the Dorion report, which was a very serious report indeed.
What respect can the people of Canada have for the administration of justice when one considers the Rivard affair, how he escaped and how he was hustled off to the United States when finally found in Canada? We do not know whether a proper extradition hearing was held. What respect can the Canadian people have for the administration of justice in view of this kind of nonsense?
I would ask the Minister of Justice to walk along the streets and ask the people what they think of the administration of justice in this country. I tell the minister that respect has never been at a lower ebb at any previous period. Where are the Lapointes, the St. Laurents, the Fultons and the Flemings, men who gave respect to this department, men who were strong and could rise above political situations? What the government needs today is a Minister of Justice-again I say this not by way of criticism of the present minister-who can rise above narrow political expediency, one of the same class who have won respect in Great Britain and in our own country. We need a man who can make his own decisions respecting the administration of the law regardless of political expediency even though those decisions affect our Liberal friends, our Conservative friends or any friends we have.
I say that the administration of justice must rise above narrow parochialism and provincialism. But what respect for the administration of justice can the Canadian people have in view of the Marcoux affair, the Dorion report and the Rivard affair?
Let me come to another affair which almost adds comedy to the whole situation and which has reduced the administration of justice to its lowest level in our history. Let us consider the whole sordid affair in connection with Banks. He was charged and convicted. Then he was granted bail. The government said it was the judiciary who let him out on bail. Then for weeks we questioned the government regarding his whereabouts. But no one knew where he was. Today we pick up the

Mr. Chairman, I hope it is not unreasonable on my part to emphasize the
February 24, 1966

fact that this is my first intervention in the debate from a new geographical position in the chamber. Since the traffic in party warfare does not appear to be as heavy or as loud as on other occasions I am tempted to seek the indulgence of the committee, which I understand is traditionally granted on the occasion of a maiden ministerial address, particularly when estimates are being dealt with. I ask to be allowed a little more leeway than perhaps is normal. On most occasions I attempt to address the house with few notes but since I am now dealing with estimates I ask the indulgence of the committee to refer to them in close detail.
The hon. member for Bow River raised a very fair question as to the division of responsibility between the Minister of Justice and myself. May I say to him, with great respect, that I believe the Prime Minister tabled orders in council under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act under which certain responsibilities heretofore assigned to the Department of Justice, namely, the penitentiary service, the National Parole Board and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, have been assigned to the office of the Solicitor General. Hon. members will note that I used the word "office", not "department". The machinery necessary for that transformation has not yet been brought before this chamber.
Allow me to deal first of all with the penitentiary service. I wish to acknowledge with sincerity the creative plans and reforms designed by the previous administration. I am pleased to inform the house that there has been no slackening in the efforts to transform the penitentiary service into an effective and forward-looking organization which I hope will bring dividends to all of us.
Perhaps the house will allow me to strike a brief personal note. The nature of my professional life brought me in close contact with many young people who had run afoul of our criminal laws. It appeared to me at that time that penal reform should not be as difficult as some people suggested. I must candidly admit that things do not seem to me now as they seemed to me then. The reason can be explained in part by the fact that we are attempting to do two things which by their very nature appear to be in opposition to each other. In the first place, we are attempting to rehabilitate the offender so that he achieves a sense of self-respect for the rights of others. At the same time we are trying to protect society by dealing with the prisoner
Supply-Justice
with a view to deterring him and others from repeating the same offence. It is almost like riding two horses at once, an accomplishment which, I am informed, requires great skill and patience.
The task is made tremendously more difficult by the size of our prison population, the overcrowding of our institutions and the need for more research in criminology and the problem of staff recruiting. Each year the penitentiary service receives more than 3,600 inmates from the courts. On the basis of a careful study of inmate population trends in the past it is estimated that the penitentiary population will be approximately 8,500 in 1967 and 10,500 in 1973. On December 31, 1965, there were 7,362 inmates in penitentiaries, and it is disappointing and disturbing to realize that on past performance approximately 40 per cent will return after release.
There is the other side of the coin. I am glad to say that the penitentiary service is making considerable progress with the building program. During the next eight months five new medium security institutions will be opened at Springhill, Cowansville, Wark-worth, Drumheller and Matsqui, together with a start on a special correction unit at St. Vincent de Paul. The approximate cost of these institutions is $40 million.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Perhaps I should say a word about the special correctional unit under construction at St. Vincent de Paul, particularly as there has been some criticism. I should emphasize that the penitentiary service is pleased to have the views of the various associations and individuals who have an enlightened interest in this subject. The special correctional unit is not for the treatment of psychotic inmates. It is for hostile, aggressive and dangerous inmates who disrupt normal institutional programs. It is designed for a population that will not exceed 160 inmates. It incorporates training facilities with the very necessary degree of maximum security for the hostile and dangerous inmates who will be held there in detention. I am informed that the hostile type of inmate I am referring to comprises roughly 3 per cent of the present inmate population.
It is only fit and proper that I put on record that inmate training programs for the special correctional units and the design of the units were developed under the guidance of the director of inmate training, Mr. J. C. A. LaFerriere, who has had 15 years experience at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, and

February 24, 1966
Supply-Justice
Dr. Jean Garneau, an experienced psychologist, Dr. L. P. Gendreau, a psychiatrist of 18 years experience as a senior officer of the penitentiary service, and other senior officers with long experience.
Construction on three other proposed correctional units has been stayed pending the experience that will arise from the operation of the unit at St. Vincent de Paul. It is my earnest hope that the proposed joint committee on penitentiaries will be able to inspect this unit in the near future.
The program provides for the discontinuance of St. Vincent de Paul as a maximum security institution by 1970, by which time new facilities will have been built at St. Anne des Plaines. It will be a source of satisfaction to all hon. members to know that the "bucket wing" at St. Vincent de Paul will be closed in 1967.
Subject to the vicissitudes of the future, 20 new institutions will be completed to round out the 10 year plan of institutional development. The burden of success of a penal reform program rests substantially on staff. The penitentiary service is experiencing the same difficulties in recruiting as are being experienced by institutions, industries and businesses elsewhere. There is particular difficulty in recruiting psychologists and classification officers.
A survey of the penitentiary service system of pay classification by P. S. Ross and Company has been completed and is under study by the Treasury Board representatives. I am hoping that the results of this study will be made known very shortly.
Research in criminology is of prime importance, and the committee will be pleased to learn that an amount of $20,000 has been included in the budgetary estimates for the fiscal year 1966-67 to defray the cost of studies to be undertaken by the department of criminology of the University of Montreal for the benefit of the penitentiary service.
It is hoped to achieve by 1968 a universal system of custodial and training facilities in each of the four regions of Canada, so that every inmate can be kept in the degree of security he requires and can receive the training most appropriate to his needs. It is hoped that the policy that no institution should accommodate more than 450 inmates will be put in effect with the opening of five new institutions this year.
The program of penitentiary development for the fiscal year 1966-67 will see the commencement of construction of the new maximum security institution at St. Anne des

Plaines which will reduce substantially the inmate population at St. Vincent de Paul, and the construction of a new maximum security institution at Millhaven near Kingston, which in turn will make it possible to reduce effectively the inmate population of Kingston penitentiary. At Millhaven the penitentiary service will also commence construction of a reception centre to serve the Ontario region.
In addition, the penitentiary service is establishing a community release centre for women in Kingston. Properties will be acquired in the cities of Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver that will serve as community release centres. At these centres, inmates who are within two months of expiration of sentence or of release on parole will be provided with shelter, food and counselling while they are finding employment and becoming adjusted again to living again in a free community.
During 1966-67 construction of a correctional staff college will be commenced at St. Vincent de Paul for the training, both basic and advanced, of penitentiary service officers. It will be comparable in size to the correctional staff college that was opened in Kingston in 1964 where facilities are available for training up to 100 officers at a time.
Over the past 10 years some 3,000 trainees have graduated from training courses in penitentiaries and have been released to society. Only 11 per cent of them were subsequently sentenced again to penitentiaries. This is encouraging in the face of the general average of penitentiary recidivism among inmates admitted to the penitentiary system in any year which, as I said earlier, is running at approximately 40 per cent.
There is no need for me to say that I have touched but lightly on this vast and very important subject. The picture that I should like to present to the committee is one of great pressure, but not one of crisis, of expansion and not complacency. However, before I leave this subject I should say I was gravely concerned upon assuming my new responsibilities to learn that juveniles continue to be held as inmates in our federal institutions, and I must say that the hon. member for Bow River first drew my attention to this very disturbing situation in a very admirable speech approximately two years ago. At the present time I understand that there are four 15 year-olds, all in the federal training centre at Laval City, a special institution for young offenders between the ages of 16 to 23.
February 24, 1966



There are 20 inmates 16 years of age and 73 inmates 17 years of age. Teenagers are incarcerated in penitentiaries because they have committed offences under the criminal law and have been sentenced to penitentiary terms by the courts. This is usually brought about because a case has been referred by the juvenile courts to the adult courts.
The report of the departmental committee on juvenile delinquency, which was initiated by the hon. member for Kamloops, is now receiving attention in the Department of Justice and in the office of the Solicitor General, and incarceration of juveniles in penitentiaries will be one of the matters receiving close attention.
I should say a word about the National Parole Board. The staff of the national parole service was increased during the present fiscal year, or is presently being increased, by the addition of 21 new parole officers. I hope that my words will not be construed as reflecting on the members of the National Parole Board who are doing an excellent job in a very difficult and trying position. But the fact of the matter is that at the present time only a small portion of penitentiary inmates qualify for parole. In the calendar year 1964, 650 inmates, or 18 per cent of the total of 3,617 released, were granted parole. It is encouraging to note that in 1965 the number of paroles increased to 1,040 inmates, representing 28 per cent of the 3,730 inmates released from federal institutions. In other words, the great majority of penitentiary inmates are not released on parole but on expiration of their time.
Many inmates do not wish to obtain parole because they do not wish to be under supervision. They prefer to stay longer in the penitentiary and obtain complete freedom than to be released earlier but under supervision for a much longer time.
The committee will be interested to learn that the Parole Act is under active study with a view to proposing amendments that will assist in increasing the opportunities for parole.
Finally, I turn to deal with the activities of the R.C.M.P. Hon. members may be interested to learn something of the volume of work required to be done by the force in discharging its various responsibilities. I am informed that during the fiscal year which ended on March 31, 1965, for example, charges were laid by officers of the force in respect of 41,031 offences against the Criminal Code. My
Supply-Justice
information is that the total number of instances requiring investigation increased during the fiscal year 1964-65 by about 25 per cent over the previous fiscal year.
In addition to these activities the force rendered assistance to various other police forces throughout Canada in the investigation of a further 14,297 cases, most of which arose under the Criminal Code.
In general, the K.C.M.P. figures indicate that the force was called upon during the fiscal year 1964-65 to perform about 17 per cent more investigations, prosecutions and appearances than had been the case during the previous fiscal year. The figures for the fiscal year 1965-66 are not yet available but my information to this point certainly does not give any reason to believe that the work load of the force has decreased during the past 11 months.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the Solicitor General on his first presentation as minister and to say to him I believe all members of the house will wish to co-operate with him in the work he has undertaken and in bringing a progressive view into the administrative fields which are under his responsibility.
I do not intend to discuss, however, the items he has brought forward at this time. I intend to discuss what I regard as being a very grave matter affecting the administration of the Department of Justice and which in my view has constituted a major scandal. I should like to adopt the words used by the Globe and Mail of Toronto as long ago as June 14, 1963, when they referred to fraud in the field of bankruptcy as being twentieth century robbery on a grand scale.
The failure of the government of Canada and the Department of Justice in particular

to pay attention to the repeated warnings they have received of the colossal scale of fraud in this field is a sorry record of laxity, inefficiency, inadequacy and neglect not only in the legislative field but also in the field of the administration of the law as it stands. Even to this day, as I propose to show, the Minister of Justice, who I know is fairly new at his job, still has failed to accept the full responsibility which lies upon him and his department. He is practising the usual buckpassing.
We want to ask him what his reasons are for inaction in this field. What are some of the facts? I intend to give them in some detail because they present a record which I think is no less than shocking, As long ago as 1961, and maybe it happened before this, the Canadian Lumbermen's Association submitted a brief to the then Minister of Justice, the present hon. member for Kamloops. It contained detailed suggestions relating to amendment of the Bankruptcy Act and pointed out that in the year 1960-this was in 1961-defaulted liabilities had increased by 55 per cent to the figure of $148 million. I am going to point out later that in this last year they are expected to exceed $500 million. So we are not speaking of a trivial matter. The increase in 1960 was an increase of 55 per cent. The Lumbermen's Association represents some 600 members doing business all over eastern Canada. I should like the committee to note the recommendations they made roughly five years ago to the effect that the government should give full publicity to firms going into bankruptcy, particularly fraudulent bankruptcy, and any trustee irregularities. They also urged the government to increase its staff of investigators and to hire chartered accountants. This was in 1961.
In February of 1962 another association of businessmen, the Canadian Construction Association, sent a brief to the then Minister of Justice who at that time was still the hon. member for Kamloops. This association has a membership of some 1,200 firms and 61 affiliated construction associations. They claimed in their brief, with some justice, to represent a cross-section of business and industry in Canada. They referred to the growing number of bankruptcies and the prevalence of fraud and premeditation in bankruptcies. This was in February of 1962. They urged full investigation by a court approved public accountant with a view to disclosing bankruptcy offences.
In March of 1962 the Canadian Credit Men's Association, which has some 4,200
February 24, 19G6

members representing leading manufacturing, wholesale and distribution firms, sent another brief to the Minister of Justice. This brief was prepared about four years ago after consultation with the foremost bankruptcy lawyers in all parts of Canada. It refers to the large number of fraudulent bankruptcies. It recommends-I invite the attention of the committee to this-that to deal with the situation a special department should be established under the supervision of the superintendent of bankruptcy for the investigation and prosecution of bankruptcy offences. Has this suggestion been adopted? No.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
After they sent it to the hon. member for Kamloops, the then Minister of Justice, and nothing happened they waited for a while and sent it in again to a later Minister of Justice, the present President of the Privy Council. Has any action been taken in respect of those suggestions? There has been no action taken as far as I can make out.
Then in October of 1963, which I point out is now two and half years ago at least, a most highly expert and qualified group made their submission to the then Minister of Justice, Hon. Lionel Chevrier. Perhaps they hoped that with a new administration action might be expected. But they were to be disappointed. This brief was submitted by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. They referred, as I have, to the description of bankruptcy frauds as "twentieth century highway robbery on a grand scale".
They then set out what the purpose of bankruptcy is and for the benefit of hon. members I should like to read what they say in that regard. It is:
-the expeditious realization of a debtor's assets and the distribution of the proceeds among the creditors entitled to them in law-the punishment of the dishonest debtor-and the ultimate discharge of the debtor from bankruptcy and his integration into society once again freed from a crushing burden of debt.
Then they went on in their preface to the brief to say this, and this explains some of the reasons for the colossal scale of bankruptcy frauds:
Early in the committee's study, it was realized that the sales and credit policies in our highly competitive economy fostered and even encouraged an over-extension of credit. Such credit policies were entirely innocent in most instances; in others, they bordered on exploitation. This economic atmosphere was ripe for the racketeer and his strategies. Furthermore, the ease with which corporations can be formed and transfers of interest made, has created an impersonal atmosphere
Supply-Justice
in which the moral aspect of business can be easily forgotten. These facts, when examined in terms of the Bankruptcy Act, revealed that, while the Act needed certain amendments, one of the principal areas requiring corrective action was in the field of administration.
I emphasize that they suggest that action is required in the field of administration. They then summarized their proposals, which included legislative proposals, but I only want to read from the fourth suggestion in their summary where it is stated:
Suggestions for the reorganization of the office of the superintendent of bankruptcy to assist the department in its supervision of bankrupt estates and the activities of licensed trustees.
They then went on to give detailed suggestions of some of the technical problems and legislative changes that are required. I do not intend to detain the committee by going into them. However, at page 25 they deal with a subject that I am concerned about, the subject of fraud. They quote a speech of Mr. W.
J.	McQuillan, Q.C. delivered on June 19, 1959 to the Eastern Credit and Financial Management Conference and state:
My last comment will be on a subject on which any lawyer whose interests are normally identified with creditors feels very keenly. Some of you may know, having been victims, that in Montreal over the past few years, four or five organized gangs have been operating. The pattern is simple.
Then he goes on to describe the simple pattern in 1959 which he said was operating in the field of bankruptcy frauds. These remarks are quoted by the Institute of Chartered Accountants in their 1963 brief at page 26, and I invite the attention of the committee to this statement which shows the total breakdown of the administration of justice in this field. They state:
Appropriate steps are seldom, if ever, taken to bring dishonest debtors and other parties involved to justice.
I emphasize that statement made by the Institute of Chartered Accountants. They say:
Appropriate steps are seldom, if ever, taken to bring dishonest debtors and other parties involved to justice.
Then on page 27 they spell out in detail some of the things that ought to have been done and have not been done by this administration or its predecessor. They say:
For many reasons this system is unsatisfactory as:-
They refer to the system in vogue as being unsatisfactory and then list reasons as follows:
The superintendent of bankruptcy seldom takes part in investigations of alleged fraudulent actions relating to bankruptcies.

In fraudulent cases, one or a number of creditors may themselves be involved in the fraudulent action.
In fraudulent cases, by the time secured creditors are paid, there is often nothing left to finance an investigation and creditors are loathe to "throw good money after bad".
They then refer to some of the improper transaction and they state:
Deliberate omission of certain assets from the statement of affairs.
Admission by the trustee of improper claims of creditors.
Failure by the trustee to report improper acts and transactions by the bankrupt prior to bankruptcy proceedings.
Improper repossession of goods by certain creditors to the detriment of other creditors.
If all these things were known to the Institute of Chartered Accountants, what action if any has the superintendent of bankruptcy and the Department of Justice taken in respect of these matters? They then make several suggestions of things that should be done. These are in the form of recommendations and the first one is:
The position of superintendent of bankruptcy is of sufficient importance to justify the status of assistant deputy minister.
The staff of the superintendent should be strengthened by the appointment of three assistants whose duties would be to supervise:
Activities of registrars, official receivers and trustees; investigations of bankruptcy frauds; processing of trustees' statements.
Item 5 in their recommendations is:
The superintendent of bankruptcy should assume the responsibility, financial and otherwise, of conducting investigations where there is evidence of fraud.
I intend to point out later that this Minister of Justice, and perhaps he will deal with this later, has several times asserted that this is not the responsibility of his department.
In October of 1964 the government of the province of Quebec instituted an inquiry known as the Mercier inquiry which reported on July 30, 1965. This inquiry was largely concerned with loss of revenue to the provincial department of revenue in bankrupt estates, but the inquiry was expanded and found, and I invite the attention of the committee to this:
The inquiry directed by this commission revealed a very deplorable if not alarming situation which existed in bankruptcy and liquidation matters in Quebec.
Then on page 7 of the report it is stated that the inquiry demonstrated that dishonesty and fraud deeply penetrated in one way or another a large proportion of bankruptcies and liquidations. I invite the attention of the committee to these words to be found in the

official report to the legislature and the government of the province of Quebec. It states that the underworld did at the same time a lucrative business to the detriment of honest creditors.
In October of 1965 the Canadian Lumbermen's Association returned to the attack. You will remember that they filed a brief pointing out all these things in 1961. Four years later they thought they might try again, and they stated that fraudulent bankruptcies in the lumber industry in Quebec alone amounted to some $46 million. They then added this view which is the result of an inquiry by their members over seven months through a special committee they had set up:
-this sordid situation has links with political campaign funds, narcotics peddling and arson swindlers.
That is not the view I express; it is a view put forward in a brief after investigation by this association of businessmen. Then the Globe and Mail in dealing with the submission of the Lumbermen's Association said, reporting the chairman of the committee:
It had been trying in vain for several years to get action from the federal and Quebec governments. It asked Prime Minister Pearson for a royal commission in February 1964.
The Globe and Mail then stated that Mr. Leblanc, who I assume was the chairman of the committee, had said:
We have the impression of watching a football game between federals and provincials, where the two teams are stalling the game and throwing on each other the responsibility for doing so.

Mr. Kierans, then the revenue minister for Quebec, did not agree with this description. In a speech to the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association in the fall of 1965 he accused the federal Department of Justice of hindering Quebec's war on the bankruptcy underworld. I should like to know whether Mr. Kierans was making a responsible or an irresponsible statement when he said that the federal Department of Justice was hindering Quebec's war on the bankruptcy underworld. I think a committee of this house should be interested in this matter too.
Mr. Kierans said that Quebec-he meant the government of Quebec-had complained to the federal department for years about laxity and loopholes in the Bankruptcy Act and was now insisting that Ottawa act. Those are the words he is quoted as having used. The present minister may say that he has only been in office for a short time and that he now proposes at long last, after these years of
February 24, 1966

responsible demonstrations of a substantial scandal, to do something about it. But unfortunately he has been in office long enough to demonstrate a settled determination to avoid the issue.
I should like to quote what the minister is reported to have said. This is in the Heavy Construction News, a newspaper published by the construction industry, of September 24, 1965. If I am misquoting the minister I have no doubt he will correct me.
"The real complaint is that certain people are obtaining credit unscrupulously with no intention of or likelihood of meeting their debts after disposing of the goods they obtain." Cardin-
That is the familiar way in which they refer to the minister:
Cardin said: "Bankruptcy is the inevitable result but it usually is the consequence of what has been done, rather than a means in itself of defrauding creditors. The suppression of pre-bankruptcy fraud is the responsibility of the provincial authorities as a part of the administration of criminal justice by the provinces" he emphasized.
"The federal role, on the other hand, exercised through the superintendent of bankruptcy, has always been understood to be especially the supervision of the trustees".
In these words, as I read them, the Minister of Justice is rejecting the emphatic, documented, reasoned pleas of all the business organizations I have quoted, namely, that the superintendent of bankruptcy should take responsibility for the investigation and if not the detailed prosecution at least the preparation of the prosecution of these offences.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member wants to be fair and I believe it would be useful if I said something here, if he would permit me to do so. It is true that the federal government is responsible for the administration of bankruptcy. The superintendent can in fact initiate investigations; but the actual prosecution and investigation of any criminal activity in this field as in any other field and the administration of the Criminal Code are under the provincial authorities. This is all I meant to say in that statement.
We do not claim that we have no responsibility for the administration of bankruptcy. We claim that we do not have the responsibility for actually investigating and prosecuting criminal charges that might arise within a bankruptcy.

I am glad to hear the minister's explanation but unfortunately it does not jibe with what he is alleged to have said;
Supply-Justice
at least, I do not think it does. The Canadian Press in an article in the Globe and Mail of February 10 last quoted the minister in this way:
Justice Minister Lucien Cardin said such investigations-
Investigations into bankruptcy frauds.
-are a provincial matter. The federal government was responsible only for the supervision of bankruptcy trustees.
What I am trying to point out to the minister is that all these organizations, the Institute of Chartered Accountants, the Canadian Construction Association, the Canadian Lumbermen's Association, the Canadian Credit Men's Association, have for years been urging that the responsibility which is in the act be carried out by the superintendent of bankruptcy by setting up a staff adequate to deal with this colossal cancer on our society.
I suggest that instead of putting forward these evasive statements and shoving the responsibility off to the provinces, the minister should accept this responsibility and take steps to solve this very difficult situation. The minister does not have to tell me, because I happen to be a lawyer trained in this field and know it very well, that the prosecution of these matters rests with the provinces. I also know that in narcotics and combines cases the federal authorities provide counsel because they know these are difficult matters. They take their responsibility seriously in these cases. But these bankruptcy frauds are not being taken seriously.
I am not blaming the minister for this, but the miniscule staff available to deal with these situations is totally inadequate. They are not able to deal with racketeers of the type who are defrauding the Canadian public on a colossal scale year after year. Nothing is done by the government that is responsible for this matter. I say to you, Mr. Minister, through the Chairman that it is time we stopped using provincial responsibility as an excuse for inaction in this matter. The field of bankruptcy is clearly defined in section 91 of the British North America Act to be the responsibility of the federal government.
I hope we are not going to see more and more abandonment of federal responsibility in jurisdiction. That this matter should be dealt with adequately by the government and the Department of Justice is essential for the protection of businessmen across Canada. These gangsters or criminals are smart enough to use provincial boundaries in hopping from one place to another. We need a

February 24, 1966
Supply-Justice
nationally effective administration, properly staffed with accountants and so on, to deal with this matter.
I hope we will never again hear in the house the statement by the responsible minister that these investigations are just a provincial matter and the federal government is only responsible for the supervision of bankruptcy trustees. I remind the minister, if the government is responsible for the supervision of bankruptcy trustees, that according to the Institute of Chartered Accountants in 1963 many of these trustees are themselves appointed by fraudulent creditors. Many of them do not do their jobs and supervision has been inadequate. We need an entirely different approach in this field to anything we have had in the past.
What does the minister do? He says we will have some amendments to the act. Well and good. Then four years later we are still told we are to have some amendments to the act and the question will be considered by a new group of lawyers. The Institute of Chartered Accountants and the construction industry consulted lawyers expert in this field four years ago. They could sit down with the officials of the department capable of understanding and explain the changes necessary in the law. I suggest also, Mr. Chairman, that this house contains enough competent people who could advise the government in this regard. Why appoint one lawyer in Montreal, one in Toronto and one in Ottawa? I do not know whether they are friends of the administration and need something to do but I do not believe it is necessary to put off these things in this way. There has been a terrible neglect in this field. Again I say that the minister should not bear the brunt of the blame for this situation; it has been happening for quite a long time.
I hope the amendments to the act will be referred to the Justice Committee and that the committee will take the responsibility not only of looking into the amendments proposed but inquiring into the administration, which the Institute of Chartered Accountants said was of crucial importance in this field.
I suggest that the tale of governmental and departmental waiting in this field requires a more searching scrutiny. What is wrong with the department? What is wrong with its administration? For five years they have been investigating this subject. For five years they

have received a flood of complaints and detailed suggestions poured forth from responsible business organizations. I will never again complain that the Liberal government is too subservient to business interests because apparently they are prepared, at least if small businessmen are concerned, to ignore completely the very rational suggestions made to them. It is an unjust accusation for anybody to make that they pay any attention to the needs of business because apparently they do not.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, for five years they have heard these complaints and millions, indeed hundreds of millions, of dollars have been lost by these repeated frauds. The laws designed to protect honest debtors have been used as instruments of fraud. Thousands of businessmen all across Canada have lost legitimate payment for their goods. The need for action has been demonstrated time and again. The direction of the remedial action required has been clearly indicated but nothing has happened. There is something rotten here and if not rotten at least pitifully inept. In my view the committee should not only review changes in the legislation now proposed but should seek to find out why a whole succession of ministers of justice have been unable apparently to secure from the department the advice required to take the administrative and legislative steps needed to eradicate this crying scandal.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
If by any chance this matter does not seem to be of great importance to this committee, and I hope it does, then the sort of headline we saw today should remind us of the gravity of the matter. When we allow criminals to get involved in matters like bankruptcy with great profit to themselves, then it follows as day follows night that honest men will find themselves shot because they had the guts to fight but did not have adequate help from the government in the past. I hope they will have that help in the future in dealing with this major injustice and fraud on the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity of addressing a few words to the committee in connection with the field of justice-or perhaps I should now say fields of justice, and the various components into which, I think regrettably, it is in the process of being divided. I want to make it clear that while I intend to confine myself to some fairly general remarks at this stage I do so only because it seems clear there will be
February 24, 1966

other more appropriate opportunities to go into discussion in depth and in detail on other questions when the main estimates for
1966-67 are being considered. Nethertheless I have some observations which while of a general nature deal with matters of sufficient importance that it is desirable to make them at this time. I am not going to follow in detail the line of the hon. member who has just spoken, but I want to refer before I conclude to one aspect of bankruptcy.
The subject which concerns me most at the present time is the proposal to divide the responsibilities formerly discharged by the Department of Justice into three. I want to make it clear also that I make no criticism of the Solicitor General personally. I am sure we all appreciated the brief resume he gave us this afternoon of the work he is undertaking and his approach to it. It is not with respect to his capabilities personally that I am concerned. I am sure we all look forward to the time, if the government's proposal is adopted, when he will bring his considerable and extensive capabilities to the discharge of his new responsibilities.
But I do not believe the responsibility should be divided. I assure you, sir, that I have attempted to keep an open mind, but I am satisfied on the basis of my own experience that it is a mistake to divide these functions as it is now proposed to divide them. I am sure of my ground when I say that what is needed in this field is not more division but more and better co-ordination. My view is that co-ordination will become more and more difficult, if not impossible, to achieve when you have this clear, sharp distinction which it is now proposed to create between the functions of the respective ministers amongst whom this work is to be divided.
I base my position on my own experience, the experience I had during the course of my administration of the department and upon the more recent experience of the present government. I do not want, sir, to claim any special farsightedness or any personal credit for the very good relationships which existed between the various branches, services and components of the Department of Justice that characterized the years between 1957 and 1963. But it was not accidental. I am not seeking to reflect on anybody. I am stating it as a fact that this condition was not in existence in June of 1957.
What we found then was that there was too great a tendency for the various services to operate without adequate knowledge of what the other services were doing. They would,
Supply-Justice
therefore, frequently be working at crosspurposes. I am quite certain, Mr. Chairman, that in no field is it more important than in this field that there be co-ordination. You cannot have the enforcement section operating in a vacuum from the correction section, with policies not co-ordinated, and above all you cannot have the enforcement and correction branches operating in a vacuum and without co-ordination with the administrative and law-making functions. We initiated administrative procedures during those years which would make it certain that there was co-ordination, co-ordination with respect to administration, co-ordination with respect to the passage of information between the R.C.M.P., the penitentiaries service, the parole functions and the administrative and lawmaking functions, all of which came within the scope of the department and the Minister of Justice as he then exercised the responsibilities.
It was a very happy experience and I am satisfied I am stating the matter correctly when I say that the officers of the department who reported to the minister all appreciated the fact that there was this co-ordination. I leave that there, Mr. Chairman. I say next that I am quite satisfied that if there had continued to be that co-ordination, that exchange of information, some of the grievous, far-reaching mistakes that have characterized the administration of justice under the present government, especially in the years from 1963 to 1965, would not have happened because they could not have happened.
I do not want to rehearse all the difficulties surrounding the position of the President of the Privy Council and leading up to the Dorion Commission report, but I am as satisfied as if I had been there that the difficulties in which the then Minister of Justice found himself would not have arisen, the mistakes he made would not have been made, had there been the necessary co-ordination between the R.C.M.P. and the information they were bringing the minister on the one hand and the advice the officers of the Department of Justice were there to provide on the other hand.
It was simply because the officials of the Department of Justice did not have adequate information and access to the R.C.M.P. reports that that far-reaching and grievous mistake was made in a matter affecting the basic structure and functions of representative government itself. The report on these matters received from the R.C.M.P. was not

reviewed as it should have been by officers of the Department of Justice who were there for that very purpose. So the minister in a matter of the gravest consequences, having far-reaching political consequences, placed himself in a position where he made a decision on his own without the advice which he should have taken and which would automatically have come had there been that system in effect which I have described.
I would have thought this government would have learned from its mistake. Instead, what do we see? We see a greater compart-mentalization system being built up under which there will be less and less knowledge by the one hand of what is being done by the other.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I am satisfied now-and I became satisfied as a result of the experience I had-that it is not sufficient to leave this matter of co-ordination and co-operation between the various services which report to the one minister, to a matter of mere administrative arrangement within the ministers' office. My experience convinced me that something more formal was required, and so we were working on a proposal which would result in a formal recommendation for a departmental reorganization which would both reflect the need and ensure the fact of co-ordination and co-operation. I should like to summarize that proposal here.
In my view, what is required is that we should have three deputy ministers made responsible for these functions. They would continue to be under the responsibility of one minister but there should be three deputies: A deputy in charge of administration, a deputy in charge of enforcements and a deputy in charge of corrections, all three deputies reporting to the one minister. The situation then would be that there would be one minister who, with the advice and assistance of the deputy in charge of administration -who should be given the responsibility for co-ordinating and reporting on policy to the minister-would assume the over-all responsibility in the government for the co-ordination of that policy.
It may very well be asked of me, "Why didn't you do it"? I think the answer is clear. I said that I became satisfied that this question should not be left to a mere administrative arrangement carried on by individual ministers, but should be reflected in an arrangement which assured co-ordination and

co-operation. However, political circumstances overtook us before it was possible to make a firm recommendation. Therefore I make no apology for saying this after the event.
I am making this suggestion now because the matter is of such importance that I hope the government will reconsider the organization of the work that we are discussing along those lines. Rather than bifurcating, or I think it is trifurcating the department-or as my hon. friend from Bow River has perhaps less euphemistically but more accurately described it, "creating divisive confusion"-I hope that the government will reconsider its proposals in this field and adopt a policy of co-ordination rather than division.
There are many other reasons for this suggestion apart from the obvious necessity of co-ordination and co-operation. After all, what do we see now? Apparently there is an intention to make the President of the Privy Council responsible for much, if not all, of the work in the constitutional field, at any rate as far as it lies within the sphere of dominion-provincial relations. But who is or should be the constitutional adviser to the government? Surely it is the Minister of Justice.
It is a mistake then, because of some temporary situation which may arise, some temporary difficulty in which the government finds itself, to take away these responsibilities and entrust them to others without really thinking of the over-all implications and where they will lead us in the long run.

I think we are all stirred and disturbed about the bankruptcy situation. I think too that the hon. member would not mind if I were to continue along the line he took and point out that, although we are justified in being indignant about the situation, it is a situation which seems to me to have little application to the present Minister of Justice.

I am not one to defend ministers. I never was. I agree with what the hon. member had to say and with what was said in the briefs he read from the Lumbermen's Association, namely, that a great deal of the blame must fall on trustees, on creditors, and on lawyers, though they were never mentioned, as well as on fraudulent debtors.
If I heard him correctly, the hon. member said there was no reason in the world why inspectors on the staff of the federal government could not control these trustees. Let us carry this a step further. Let us suppose such control is exercised. There will be no need to go to Quebec or to British Columbia to find out what the reaction will be. It will be forthcoming right here in Ontario. What will the Law Society of Upper Canada have to say? What will the professional organization of the chartered accountants have to say? I think the idea is a fine one. I believe it has merit. But before results can be achieved there is an even greater problem to be solved. As the hon. member pointed out very well in a speech he made during a discussion on the constitution, this is the test, a test which should be applied now by the provinces in connection with co-operative federalism.
My remarks will be directed to many other fields connected with the whole concept of justice. Co-operation has to be established generally if we are to achieve anything as a result of the work of the department in criminal investigation and in the attack on organized crime.
I was not surprised to find some reaction to the proposal to split the department into two. I admire this move. I think this is reform because at least it is a change. I hope it is done properly. I am all for change. The minister would agree with me that change is one of the most difficult things to introduce, because all those who know and rely on the old establishment are enemies of change and doubtful about what their position will be under a new system.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Reform will have to come. Is there any doubt in anyone's mind today that we do have organized crime? I think the evidence suggests that crime has now entered into fields it has never entered before. It is mobile. It is international. Yet we are trying to deal with it on the basis of very old concepts of police work and law. This is why it will be necessary to introduce changes. We are going to see organized crime in the field of bankruptcy, as has been pointed out. There is
February 24, 1966

some evidence of organized crime in the liquor business. We see it in the business of usury, in the traffic in narcotics. We see it in those elements of our business life which, though perhaps not strictly illegal, are quasimoral. We are likely to find heavy pressure put on us to legalized sweepstakes. This will invite that element of society. We are going to have pressure brought to bear upon us to legalize the whole idea of birth control measures. Again, it does not take much to imagine where crime will move in that field and we shall have to come back forcefully with new techniques.
As the hon. member for Kamloops pointed out, we have a division between the local, provincial and federal police forces but with the multiplicity of crime today we need closer co-operation between those forces. We depend on the local police force to give us the immediate information and we need the centralized R.C.M.P. to exercise their administrative powers to provide greater co-operation.
We shall have to change laws and we shall have to accept such changes in laws. We shall have to accept changed techniques in police work and we shall have to adapt our laws to those new techniques. Privacy may be lost. The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam has been disturbed about incidents connected with a person's freedom but we will have to face this problem and deal with it in such a way that we preserve the individual's freedom while at the same time allowing new methods of police work.
We shall have to introduce new methods that will keep pace with the sophistication of crime because criminals are not slouches any more. They are very jet age and we cannot stop them with old theories and old techniques. The police may have to use listening and radio devices that will interfere with privacy.
We shall have to introduce legislation dealing with the fourth estate to prevent the press from publishing things damaging to the individual. We shall have to get accustomed to the idea that freedom will have to be protected in ways different from those used in another age.
Today there are about a dozen manufacturers of machines such as lie detectors. I am given to understand on good authority that using new techniques and equipment, including drugs, we can find out the truth or falsehood of any statement. This is a scientific fact but we still depend on 12 men serving as a jury to decide between truth and falsehood. Even 12 first class psychiatrists cannot do
Supply-Justice
that as well as machines can; yet our laws prohibit the use of those machines.
We shall also need greater respect for police forces and police administrators, but that respect cannot be forced. It must come naturally. We can understand journalistic pride in stories appearing in the press but our police forces require good public relations. However, they do not employ even the semblance of public relations officers.
All this will be for nothing unless we seriously tackle the question of penal reform and rehabilitation. We are really doing nothing if 41 per cent are still repeaters, as pointed out by the Solicitor General. Today we spend more on shoes and boots for prisoners than we do on research and rehabilitation, and from what I understand the prisoners do not walk anywhere, except on the odd occasion.
We shall have to co-ordinate our efforts with those of the United States. There the position is no better. Just recently an article was published by two psychiatrists, a brother and sister team who, working at their own expense, found that they can predict criminal tendencies in children as young as seven and eight years. Their findings can be verified to an accuracy of almost 80 per cent. These two doctors have worked on their own and we do nothing to support them.
We shall have to co-ordinate all these efforts. We need qualified people. I think the minister is doing a fine job. I like him personally and I defend his position. I think we can trust him to do a good job.

I am not sure I will live that long. As my friend has said, there is a serious problem in regard to charitable donations which has been under consideration for a number of years. There have been instances in Canada, and I do not attach them to any
February 24, 1966

area or charitable organization, where some abuses have occurred in the past. Over the past several years our department has tried in several ways to tighten up the administration so that people can claim the actual amount they contributed, no more and no less. There have been a few instances, as a matter of fact, where we have had to prosecute people for issuing fraudulent receipts.
Under the existing statute there is provision for allowing individuals to claim a deduction, a flat deduction of $100. There is also a provision which allows them to claim any amount of donations actually made up to 10 per cent. As my hon. friend knows, this is not an amount that is allowed in every case; it has to be substantiated. I should like to support my department by saying that in no instance have we disallowed receipts for charitable donations without having some basis on which to arrive at the conclusion that the receipts issued by certain charitable organizations recognized under the Income Tax Act have been in excess of the actual amount of money received.
In instances where we have disallowed claims for donations we have gone to the people who have issued the receipts and asked them on what basis the receipts were issued. When the answer had been that the receipts were issued on the basis of a taxpayer's statement that he had given that much money we have questioned this and asked whether the individual representing the recipient was willing to vouch for the fact that the taxpayer had actually given that amount of money. When the individual involved, the officer in charge of the recipient charitable organization, said he would not give that kind of confirmation because receipts may have been issued in excess of the amount received we have disallowed the claim. We have always considered each individual case on its own merits.
In cases where we have disallowed a taxpayer's claim we have taken the cases to the charitable organizations involved and asked whether they would agree that the amount of money claimed was actually donated. If confirmation is forthcoming we have allowed the complete claim for the donation.
The Carter commission, which has been studying taxation laws in Canada, has been looking into the matter of charitable donations in Canada. Perhaps as my hon. friend suggests it might be better that we have some sort of over-all amount beyond the $100 and 23033-110

Supply-National Revenue allow taxpayers to claim that amount of money as charitable donations.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)

However, I should like to impress upon the hon. member for Lapointe that it is the duty of my department to administer the statute as it has been enacted by the Parliament of Canada. It is the duty of my department to make sure that people pay the taxes they are obliged to pay under the statutes and yet treat them as fairly as we can.
Over the past two years since I have been minister I have received many letters from the hon. member for Lapointe.
