Mr. Chairman, I want to raise one small matter on these estimates. It has bothered me for some time and I should like to draw it to the minister's attention. The matter I refer to relates to the low bid system for the carriage of rural mail.
In essence I have no objection to the system because I think it is the correct one and the best that can be devised. The difficulty that arises, arises after tenders are called for mail carriage on a rural route and one tender is so much lower than the others that it is quite obvious that something is wrong with the tender. When such a low tender is received either the person tendering does not know what he is doing and has no knowledge of estimating his costs or he is tendering purposely low in the hope of getting the contract and then applying to the department for an increase. These two situations cause difficulty.
With respect to the first situation where a man does not know what he is doing, I have had occasion in the past to point out several times to the Post Office Department that the low bidder could not do the job and that sooner or later he would either have to abandon his service or else operate such a poor service that the department would be forced to step in. The low bid system has resulted in the authorities saying, "Well, we are sorry but we have to accept the low bid tender. We do not see anything wrong with the man. Nobody knows of anything wrong with his character and therefore we shall have to assume that he knows what he is

DEBATES	February 24, 1966
doing". I think in cases like that the department ought not only to look at the matter twice but the department should in some cases refuse to accept that low tender. I know of several instances where the department has accepted such a tender, the job has been poorly done and eventually the contractor has had to get out, with resultant bad service for a period of weeks or even months. One reason for such low tenders is bad estimating by the tenderer.
Second, sometimes when a person wants to get a contract he hopes he can carry it at a loss for two years, after which time he will apply to the department for an increase. In such cases the department often grants an increase. I think that the position of the department with respect to any contractor who receives a contract through unfair competition by bidding too low should be that such a person should not be given an increase for at least the full term of four years of his contract. I know that in some cases where an increase has been awarded after two years the result has been to the detriment of those people who made a bona fide bid on a fair estimate of the job, because the initial contractor making the low bid took a loss for two years and then was awarded the normal scale again.
I wish to point this out because in both cases I think a contract ought to be refused. It ought to be refused if one bid is a great deal lower than other bids. If in accordance with calculations it is shown that the bid is far too low, the contract should not be given to the tenderer making that low bid.
I have come across this situation several times and I want to draw it to the minister's attention as a policy matter that ought to be considered. Similar problems arise in the Department of Public Works but that is not the concern of this department. The same thing arises where an unreasonably low bidder gets a job. The result is a terribly poor job. It is exactly that sort of thing that happens in the Post Office Department.
I would urge the department to be more careful and to reject these unusually low bids that are obviously not well considered or not bona fide.

One of the arguments which has always been brought forward is that it would be pretty expensive, that the government does not have the money to pay $100, and so on, in the form

of an old age pension to everyone in this country. I would like the Minister of Veterans Affairs to pay particular attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke. I would like to add that today we have veterans who have served in the last two world wars, and I think if anybody needs consideration and special attention, they are the ones who need it at the moment.
I know that those who have pensions possibly have pensions which do not permit them to have an easy existence or at least they find themselves in the position where they have difficulty living with the pensions which they do obtain. But whether or not they have pensions, these people have served the country. Some of them were overseas for four or five years; they were the ones at that time who actually went over there and risked their skins for us. At that time we called them heroes and today we have a tendency to forget this. While they were overseas working for $1.40 or $2.00 a day, at that time we were here and perhaps had the privilege of taking the best war positions available at that time which paid very good salaries and had the opportunity to establish a future for ourselves-those who were here at that time.
While some of our colleagues, or brothers, and even sisters-but I am speaking particularly about the men-were out at the front, they were there defending their country. I think they have given us the service we had asked of them. We appreciated it at that time. It would be a mark of recognition if we return that service. I believe that one way of doing this would be what I would suggest to the minister today, and that is that, whether or not these people have a pension, they be eligible to obtain the old age pension at age 60 without a means test.
If they lost five years or so from their lives risking their own skins to defend our nation, I think we should do this for them; they are not a majority in the country. I think this would be well regarded by all citizens and that the nation might accept the idea of giving these people at least the benefit of the five years which they gave their country, in the best years of their lives. I would like the minister to take this suggestion under consideration.
I will not speak any longer on this subject during these estimates, but will wait for the new estimates. However, I would certainly appreciate it if the minister would give serious consideration to the suggestion that the government should not invoke the argument

that we do not have the means to give everybody $100, and so on. Let us start at the moment by giving all the veterans who have reached age 60 their old age pension without a means test. You might say this is an exception to the rule. Yes, but they were the exception when they had to go over there in 1914-18 and 1939-45 to defend their country. They have done their share and it is up to us to defend them when they need it so much.

With the present day high cost of living and the rapid escalation of costs at this time there is a very heavy burden and financial handicap on these mothers and their families. Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a word or two about this item in the way of a suggestion to the minister. In my experience I have found there are many veterans of world war II who enlisted in the service at about age 18 and served four or five years overseas, or practically the whole period of the war. Many of them were discharged as being fit at age 25 or 26. As a result of there being no medical disability recorded in their documents they are not eligible for pension or war veterans allowances.
In many cases these men are not and have not been able to cope with civilian life in that they are not properly trained to obtain jobs which would allow them to provide themselves and their families with a reasonable living. Much of this difficulty stems from the stress and strain they experienced during their service and, of course, from the fact that they were trained from a young age as soldiers and are not now properly trained to fit into the economy and re-establish themselves in our civilian way of life. I do not refer to people who have been assisted under the Veterans Land Act or who benefited from special considerations which allowed them to attend university or vocational schools. I refer to the group that did not benefit from any of these excellent schemes who now have difficulty obtaining suitable employment.
I suggest that some assistance should be given to this type of individual in the way of job procurement and guidance in obtaining suitable jobs. I do not suggest that they be given special financial assistance, but that they be helped in obtaining suitable employment through the Department of Veterans Affairs, as such, or in co-ordination with the efforts of the National Employment Service. While it is true that veterans have a preference in civil service competitions, many of these veterans do not wish to become civil servants or perhaps cannot qualify for the positions. They are anxious to obtain assistance in gaining employment in areas in which they live, and I think an effort along

speechtext:
In that event, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks in connection with the estimates of this department. I am fully conscious of the fact that before too long we will have an opportunity to consider the estimates for the 1966-67 fiscal year. I am sure we will also have the opportunity of considering some items of legislation in connection with the ARDA program, during which time we will be allowed to express our opinions.
Let me emphasize the fact that this whole field of forestry receives a limited amount of attention in connection with the affairs of this country, considering its importance to our general economy. At the time of the formation of this department I am sure recognition was given to the fact that much of the activity of the department would be devoted to research and practical needs. I am sure that the federal authorities considered that much of the work of this department would be carried out in conjunction with efforts of the provincial governments, inasmuch as the provinces have control over much of the timberlands, by virtue of provincial control of natural resources. I am sure that the provincial governments have a great deal of indirect influence also, in respect of privately owned timberlands situated in the provinces. It was with that sort of conception that the department came into being, and with the additional knowledge that forestry land contributes raw material to a very large industry in this country, which in turn contributes to a very important extent to the general revenue of the nation.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
I have always been amazed by the fact that the export of newsprint in dollars and cents represents one of our greatest single exports. So from the standpoint of preservation and conservation the federal government has naturally a very great interest in forestry. In consequence, Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister deserves and should receive a great deal of co-operation in connection with his most important duties. So far as I am concerned, to the extent of my capability I shall be glad to give him that co-operation at all times.
The ARDA program is also under the minister's control, as is forestry. There is a similarity perhaps in these two programs because in many instances the development
February 24, 196G

of a good deal of the land in Canada is achieved by a crop of trees. Speaking generally about the forestry industry from one end of the country to the other, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, it makes a great contribution to direct employment, indirect employment and helping to solve our balance of payments problem by reason of the fact that we to a great extent export the products of the forest. All in all, Mr. Chairman, I believe these factors make this a most important department. For this reason I believe the minister is entitled to receive from everyone the greatest possible co-operation and assistance.
Looking at the items included in these estimates I find there is the question of forest research and forest products research. It is not my intention to try to elaborate on those subjects; I believe they are understood. I do wish to say, however-and I speak with a great deal of knowledge of this particular point-that I consider the officials of the forestry department at the federal level to be second to none. They are capable and dedicated and I found it a very pleasant duty to work with them. I know the minister is conscious of this fact but I should like to say that I have a great deal of respect for the deputy minister and all the officials of the forestry department.
I might mention at this time, Mr. Chairman, in a general way the programs which the federal government shares with the provinces. I believe they come under about five different headings. One of these programs is that concerned with securing and maintaining a forest inventory. I am quite sure all hon. members will agree with the proposition that to know what we have by way of acreage in forest lands is a very important thing, but I am sure we also need to know what is growing in these areas. In conjunction with the provinces the federal government is concerned with securing inventories and in this way the Department of Forestry is able to maintain up to date figures.
Another matter of concern to this department is that of reforestation, which is perhaps not so important in the province from which I come. It does not seem that reforestation there is necessary because natural reforestation will take care of the situation very well. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the question of forest fire protection because I believe we should protect to the greatest extent possible this most important asset which is essential to our economy. We must protect our forests
Supply-Forestry
from fires and, of course, from pests. The more effective control of pests is achieved through research. With regard to forest fire protection, we find that each year we make progress in this direction. We become more efficient in fighting and combatting forest fires for the simple reason that I believe people are becoming more and more conscious of the value of our forests.
The products of our forests are not only valuable to the lumberman but to people interested in wildlife, fishing and recreation. I cannot speak with stronger feelings about the need to preserve this great natural asset which is now under the control of the minister.
Another point I should like to bring to his attention concerns the question of access roads construction in the provinces. This program is carried on by the federal government in conjunction with the provincial governments. It is my opinion that greater publicity should be given to the access roads program and the fact that it is contributed to by the federal government. The purpose of this program is to make hitherto inaccessible areas accessible. When access roads are constructed it is possible to bring timber out to the pulp or lumber mills. However, Mr. Chairman, I believe that in a good many instances in a good many provinces it is not known to the industry in general that this program for the construction of access roads is available.
I would suggest to the minister that at the appropriate season of the year he urge the provincial governments to publicize to the industry in general the fact that a program of this nature is available, and people concerned in the forest industry should be asked to submit applications pointing out where roads might be constructed in order that timber might be made more accessible than heretofore. There are areas in which it is not economical to harvest the timber but if an access road were built, to which the federal government contributes 50 per cent of the cost, the operation might become economically feasible. I suggest that the minister consider this point.
Next I should like to deal briefly with the question of stand improvement. I believe stand improvement is most important because in so many instances-and I know something about this matter from personal knowledge- we need to weed out trees in much the same way as we need to weed out carrots in the garden in order to grow a large, full crop. This has to be done in connection with stand

improvement and trees, just as it must be done in the garden but on a different scale. In my opinion programs of this type in regard to an industry which contributes and will continue to contribute to the economic life of this country are acknowledged by all of us to be very important.
As I said at the outset of these remarks, Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention t.o speak at length at this time. When the minister's estimates for the next fiscal year come before us I shall then have the privilege of making some suggestions to him, which I hope he will consider.
So far as I am concerned, the minister has always been extremely kind, courteous and anxious to help. I appreciate the co-operation I have received from him. The minister has always been anxious to make a definite contribution in his official capacity and in his personal capacity. I believe other hon. members will deal with the ARDA program in a little more detail. I would point out to the minister that I have not dealt with the ARDA program at length not because I do not think it is important but simply because the question of ARDA will be brought to the minister's attention very forcibly by other hon. members before the evening is over. Mr. Chairman, on February 2, the minister proved that he had not understood my speech

one bit. Mr. Chairman, I almost did not remain long enough to speak, because I got hungry for a good dish of blueberries. However, there is one matter that I feel I should raise at this time when these estimates are called, and that is the matter of ARDA.
ARDA is getting to be such a frequently used term, or word, that it is almost dangerous to bring it up, for fear that people will start yawning in your face. If there ever was a program that in the last few years has been oversold it is the ARDA program, not in the area so much of land reclamation or alternate land use but in an area that has received a great deal of publicity, and one that is extremely important in Canada today, that of community development.
I think for any members in the house who represent ridings that can be described as encompassing areas of rural poverty, ARDA must hold some singular and important hope because embodied in the ARDA concept, at least as it was originally envisaged by the Conservative government, is the belief that there are things that can be done of a constructive and progressive nature in rural areas to revive people in these depressed rural areas so that they may have reasonable hope.
I live in a constituency which, very soon after the introduction of ARDA, became concerned with this problem. As far back as two
Supply-Forestry
years ago, Prince county was declared a designated area for rural development. I think the minister knows this county. We have felt, particularly since that time, that we have good reason to hope that in the program of community development certain important things would happen.
I think, to be very honest, one of the things that has made it difficult for constructive things to happen in this area has been the great deal of fuzziness in negotiations between the federal and provincial governments; sometimes there has been some downright "buck passing." However, what concerns me most of all is twofold: First of all, I think we have waited far too long to define a clearcut policy of how community development is actually going to proceed at the very local level, with the people themselves. It seems that the whole concept of community development will never achieve very much unless communities that began to participate in this program have some idea of what kind of policy is in fact laid down by the federal authority.
Second, and equally important, and possibly even more unclear, is the problem of training competent people to carry out leadership in local areas. For quite a while now there has been talk about people designated as community development officers. It was only when we began to look around for people suitable for this job, that it was found they were an extremely rare animal. There are not many people in Canada today whom one could designate as being community development officers. In fact, I do not think that there are people being trained who would be suitable for that position.
In Prince Edward Island we have been very fortunate to have a man who could be called a pioneer, in the person of Mr. Rudy Dallenbach. He has had considerable experience, and I am happy to call him a personal friend. He has in his own very practical way begun to instil among the people of Prince Edward Island a certain confidence. That is the important thing, and the basic concept of community development. He had not any government policy to bring about this desired result.
One of the things that I feel is exceedingly dangerous, and which is increasing in the whole ARDA program, is that we are talking about bigger and bigger amounts of money. Almost one year ago now a new fund was envisaged euphemistically entitled FRED.

February 24. 1966
Supply-Forestry
I hold no quarrel with $50 million, and certainly not when it is related to a province annually looking to the federal government for assistance. What I really mean to lead up to is this that we could so emphasize this large amount of money, and others like it, that we do not take the time and trouble to think seriously about how we are going to get the tens and hundreds of people in the field who will be community development officers.
We must assume that we have no institution in Canada at the moment that can reliably prepare anyone to be a Community Development officer. In all likelihood I do not think that there is a suitable institution in North America that can provide us with this kind of trained person. Therefore I think it is necessary at the earliest possible date that the Department of Forestry and the new department of forestry and rural development envision a program for the training of community development officers. Very little will happen in Prince Edward Island or anywhere across the country unless we are going to put trained and competent people in this field.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks to the minister will be focused on two major points. The first one is to deal with this question of rejection of projects. The minister has declared in the house on several occasions that all projects under ARDA have to be submitted by the provinces.
The inference is, of course, that the federal authorities have no initiative to make suggestions or to propose projects in any province. I believe that the minister has done this from a previous commitment to himself that he is a provincial righter. In fact, from the way the operations are going on today, unwittingly, the minister has made himself into, one of the most effective anti-provincial righters that we have seen. I put this criticism to him in a particularly constructive fashion, because I am sure that he would not willingly try to destroy the initiative of a province.
Yet what actually happens? When the provinces submit proposals to the minister at Ottawa they are then met with the suggestion that the federal government officials will examine the project under consideration to see if it fits into their criteria of what the federal government has already done, and how things should be done.
You have the situation where the government of one province, under its philosophy, comes in and is ready to do things. I do not
i Mr. MacDonald (Prince).]
want to talk about socialistic philosophy because that is the province's privilege if it wishes to do it that way.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Another province believes in doing things by enlisting the tremendous enterprise of the private individual, either in reform of an individual farmer or that of a businessman or groups of businessmen. The particular cases in point to which I refer are the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba. The province of Quebec at the present time, although this is a generalization and not true in all cases, tends to look on the government as the source of inspiration. That is their right. I would support the minister and defend his right to say that the province of Quebec should carry out these projects in the way it thinks best. Yet in Manitoba which is in a similar position to Quebec as far as wealth is concerned-slightly below the national average-when we try to express a philosophy in the interests of the business world as well as of the farmers on the basis of plans put forward by competent and aggressive civil servants, we find our proposals clamped into procedures established by olficials here.
This criticism is not aimed just at this minister or this government. It has been applicable to all governments for many years. Over the years, as this country has grown and as government at both provincial and federal levels have moved increasingly into the affairs of the community, the federal government still acts as though all things had to be settled by officials here as if all wisdom was centred here in Ottawa. This attitude extends right from Treasury Board to the officials responsible for the ARDA program who are stultifying and limiting the rights of individual provinces to produce projects which will accomplish redevelopment in their own way.
By his continual statements that all projects must be proposed by the provinces the minister has unwittingly allowed a system to develop where all these proposals are put into a stereotyped form and under which the provinces are given no real freedom.
Let me go back to the original thinking which was demonstrated when I introduced the ARDA legislation. I emphasized on three occasions that the provinces were to be considered as the main proposers of projects, but that the federal government must always reserve its right to initiate projects. The reasoning is simple. We have a number of
February 24, 1966

provinces which as far as I can see will not be generating many proposals of their own. The reason is twofold. First there is the lack of finance and, second, it is the custom of their civil services to wait until someone else has come along with proposals. For these reasons I believe that when it sees an opportunity to improve certain of these areas the federal government would be well within its rights to propose projects to this end as part of the federal-provincial co-operation which is envisaged.
I would ask the minister to think this matter over. If he is trying to strengthen the provinces, as I wish to do, he should allow them the privilege of putting their proposals forward and carrying them out in their own way. The limit of the federal government's control over the provinces should be on the financial side, which is set up according to a formula. The only other question is whether or not a project comes under the broad umbrella of ARDA development or rehabilitation in any sense. I think we can trust the provinces to act within such a framework. If they do not act within this framework then it could be said by the federal government at the end of the year: You have infringed the understanding you gave. Then the chalk should be put to any future developments of that kind.
We must seek to develop real provincial autonomy. Inadvertently, I think, this has been hindered by the insistence that the schemes should come from the provinces and then meet criteria set up by officials here. In cases where provinces are strong and aggressive they can fight back. But even when they are strong and aggressive, as Manitoba and Quebec are, the criterion should be whether their projects, however they may differ in direction, are designed to result in the development of their areas.
The second matter on which I intend to speak involves the question of funds. The minister announced about a year ago that he had available $100 million, I think it was, which was to be distributed in accordance with a certain formula and that he had $50 million in respect of which no formula would be applied. I would like to urge again that as far as this $50 million is concerned the federal government take the initiative and say to some of our provinces-I am thinking now of the four Atlantic provinces: In your case we are willing to pay 75 per cent, 80 per cent or even 90 per cent of the cost of projects of this type in your area. I am sure
Supp ly-Forestry
the provinces which are reasonably near the national level of prosperity, or above it- British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Ontario, for instance-would understand if the minister were to say to them: I should like tc give to these other areas a disproportionate share of this money because they are the areas most in need of help from the ARDA program. I am bearing in mind that even though Quebec and Manitoba are below the national average as far as wealth is concerned they have aggressive governments and aggressive civil servants wno are fighting on behalf of their people.
This type of approach would, I believe, be in the spirit of ARDA and would greatly help in developing programs in the areas to which I have referred. I say this to the four Atlantic provinces with respect. But I believe the federal initiative should be used there more widely than in any other region.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is interesting to hear remarks being made about agriculture on the estimates of the Department of Forestry. The changes which have taken place in the responsibilities of this department indicate the lack of need for the development of the department in the first place. It has a number of buildings and has hired quite a large staff, but we hear very little from the forest industry about the federal

department. That is probably only to be expected.
In my opinion ARDA should be returned to the Department of Agriculture. Its very name, Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development, gives an indication of its purpose. If it were forestry rehabilitation and development it might well come under the forestry department, but it is not.
I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in his assessment of the scope and role of ARDA. Though expenditure under the program jumps from $12 million to $16 this year, I believe the program really has not started yet, and under no circumstances has it really been made a national program. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle had something to do with the vision of ARDA, and many people believed it would be a long-range program that would solve some of the problems of rural development.
Many people believed that a survey would be made of agricultural lands across the nation, that a survey would indicate the type of land that should be reforested, the type that should be added to agricultural areas, and the type that should be put into other uses. The provinces are using ARDA for the development of parks, reclaiming marshland and improving marginal land, but no real national survey has been made.
The minister and his predecessor have considered ARDA as a give-away program, for providing money for the provinces, instead of a program for agriculture, for the proper use of agricultural land, and for the rural use of land. If the minister does not believe this, then he should return to the idea of a survey, cataloguing the land in various areas, and making suggestions to the provinces for its use. It is not good enough to say, "We will approve this project in Ontario, that one in Quebec, and another one in B.C." It is of vital importance to the agricultural industry that proper use be made of all agricultural land.
The federal department has a staff capable of assessing the potentialities of various areas and deciding on programs for their development. Far-ranging progress could be made that way, instead of through municipalities and small groups of people forwarding projects for approval by the department.
When the minister of the day was first outlining ARDA he said there were many areas near Ottawa where submarginal land could be catalogued and returned to forest
February 24, 1966

production. He said this should be done on a large scale, that there would be mass displacement of people, that one man could look after several thousand acres of reforestation, that it would be a long-term project, and the outlay would be considerable. This was accepted as a good idea by the majority of people across Canada.
It was suggested that in other parts of Canada marginal land could be turned into wildlife parks. In western Canada large areas were to be amalgamated in blocks of land to provide grazing for cattle.
What happened to this project? I think the minister can be given a great deal of credit for the operations of his department, that they have stayed parochial and provincial, but even at that level it is difficult to find leaders for ARDA in rural areas, to find out the best use of a particular piece of land that is not producing suitable income for the families living on it, and how to return lands to production.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, if this is not the proposition, if ARDA really is not the long range solution for agriculture, then let us all sit down and design a new program that will provide the solution. I believe in the idea of ARDA; I believe in the concept that originated it, but I have heard some pretty crack-pot ideas come from some of the provinces. Once a project is approved in the province, automatically it is approved by Ottawa because Ottawa has no standard to put against it; either they agree with it or not, because Ottawa has not developed any projects of its own. They have depended on the provinces and even on the municipalities to do the deciding.
Agriculture, as we were told the other day by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, is in a time of crisis. I think this is true. I am not going to point out how many of the farmers are getting less than substandard wages. I think earlier the question was asked by the Minister of Finance whether he intended to go into the problem of the deficit income tax proposals. I do not know whether or not he thought about it, but certainly the Minister of Forestry, if he is going to administer ARDA, is going to have to think about it, because we have to do something for the farmers who are not able to move off the farm.
The average farmer in Canada is over 50 years of age and is not capable of being retrained, despite the fact that he violently
Supply-Forestry
opposes being retrained or moved out of his environment. For this reason, if the ARDA program is to be successful, it will have to provide a blueprint or a long range program which will give hope for the future of the agricultural industry and make possible the development of economic units in the agricultural areas so that it can re-use or redevelop all lands that are not capable of producing enough revenue to keep the farmer on the land. These lands will have to be handled in another way.
I do not know what the minister has in mind about this program; I do not know whether or not he has been interested in it. I hear that the minister is very progressive, but I have yet to see this. This is certainly the best field in which he could show that he is progressive, because I believe this is a field where there should be some development to help solve much of the problem we have in rural Canada. I think the machinery is here. There is no limit to the amount of money which can be paid under this type of scheme.
I believe if the minister really looks at the number of farmers he has helped by the rehabilitation program we already have undertaken, he will see that the price is exceptionally high for the amount of rehabilitation he has been able to provide.
I think the minister also will see that we have been able to accomplish very little in terms of redevelopment of agricultural land by use of the projects which have been paid for under ARDA to date. If the minister wishes to be progressive, if he wants to show that he is one of those three leaders from the province of Quebec who wanted to join the N.D.P. because they did not think that party could be elected and therefore joined the Liberal party instead, if he wants to get into this class, then I would like to see him start showing it. I think this is an excellent place to do it and I say this sincerely. If he really believes agriculture can be helped, that agriculture can be changed, that the redevel-lopment of marginal farms can be accomplished without major dispersement of the agricultural communities, and if he wishes to find a way to help the farmer, I think he will have to think about what a farmer is, what the family farm is, and what the relationship is between those people who live in a rural and urban economy. He will have to understand why those who are in the rural area choose that environment.
Let us not kid ourselves. Many of us choose a rural environment although we are not

February 24, 1966
Supply-Forestry
farming. Most of the developments in the suburban areas are in areas which were rural a few years ago. The fact is that people moved into the suburbs because of a desire to be in that environment and the desire not to live in somebody's backyard; but it is not the desire to live like a farmer who gets up at six o'clock in the morning, milks the cows, cleans out the henhouse, gathers the eggs, and does the other menial tasks, and then finds he has not enough money to buy the kids' shoes. It is not the lack of income which the farmer likes and it is not the work the farmer likes, but rather the environment; and in my opinion this environment will have to be improved to provide people in Canada with the choice to live in a rural environment with an opportunity to have a decent standard of living.
The minister might consider this proposition in ARDA, because we have an opportunity there where we could take some of the people in the sub-marginal areas and apply a standard of living of $3,000 net for the farmer. If he does not earn that amount, when he files his income tax we pay him; if he makes more than that, we collect from him.
This would be much better than putting the farmer off the farm. You are putting him off the farm now, not through ARDA but because of the agricultural policies of the government; and you are putting him in the city and providing him with welfare. Every person connected with municipal councils will know that in the major cities, in Ontario at least, people who are living in the city have their welfare expenses charged back to the community from where they came. The solution is not simple; it is very complicated, but I do think the federal Department of Forestry, if it wants to administer ARDA, is going to have to work nationally toward a way to deal with this problem.
We have, in agriculture, to resolve the problem of the rehabilitation and redevelopment of agricultural lands into economic units. There may be projects of the federal government of this nature which might indicate that some progress has been made to develop programs; but I have had discussions with officials under a previous minister and I am of the opinion that there was no federal plan at all in any way, shape or form, except these projects which are originated in the provinces, if they look like they are doing anything in the agricultural field or in the field of rural environment, because you certainly could not call a swamp an agricultural potential. ARDA will go in and make a wildlife park out of the proposition.
fMr. Peters.]
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
It is difficult for me to relate these things. This did not seem to bother anybody administering ARDA. I have not really been aware of any national projects they have engaged in to even set a pattern of how it was going to work. I listened with a great deal of interest years ago to the minister of agriculture who introduced this particular act. I felt at that time that his ideas were visionary and that some consideration should be given to them. I am sure the present minister will reply to the many statements of criticism that have been made in respect of the application of ARDA either during this debate or at some other appropriate time. I hope he will give us the assurance that if ARDA is to be continued it will not consist of handouts to the provinces, with handouts by the provinces in turn to the municipalities. I hope the program will be designed to fit into the redevelopment of the agricultural industry across Canada and provide some assistance to and solution for the problems of those provinces that have not yet considered the ARDA program in all its ramifications.
It is my hope that the minister will provide great leadership in this program of great potential to the agricultural communities across Canada. Surely we are aware of the problem this industry faces relating to the lack of money and the inability to establish economic units in this nation. I am sure some hon. members will disagree with me in this regard, but it seems to me that the inability of this nation to provide subsidies to agricultural producers in this country has left the majority of this portion of our population in an unattractive economic position. Surely this country should be able to provide the farmers of the nation with a reasonable standard of living equal to that enjoyed by their brothers living in urban society. This has not as yet been accomplished and can only be accomplished by a federally developed agricultural program that will make it possible for farmers to receive the greatest return possible for their efforts.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the agricultural field is one which requires economic planning. Reforestation must be taken into consideration in the over-all agricultural picture, because this really could make a difference to the farmers. They do not really care much whether they are milking cows or cutting Christmas trees, as long as they are making a decent living. I hope the minister has given this whole subject sufficient consideration and
February 24, 1966

will be able to come to the committee with plans for the future. Perhaps he will give us an added bonus by telling us whether he expects to remain with this Department of Forestry, or whether we should point our guns at another minister of another department who will in the end become responsible.

Mr. Chairman, after hearing all these questions and answers, I must say I feel this matter is almost as complicated as trying to find out who is in charge of the feed grain agency.
When you look into the matter, you almost have to look in a crystal ball in order to find out which department is responsible for it. I see here that it comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Forestry, under Item No. 10.
So, it is quite puzzling. When you want to discuss the Canadian Wheat Board, you must refer to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). For the feed grain agency, one must speak to the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), and when cultivation and agriculture are to be discussed, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) is the one to be consulted; although the two other matters concern agriculture.
It is somewhat confusing, but I hope that there will be no drastic or sudden change in the future, so that we may get used to that procedure.
I would like to make a few representations and put some questions to the minister, especially since there is nothing new about the matter. I have spoken several times about it and I think that the minister himself had the opportunity to give some explanations and even make a few corrections in the house.
We had the opportunity this week to meet the delegates of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I asked them if they had heard about the feed grain board. They had not. When the hon. member for Compton-Fron-tenac (Mr. Latulippe) put a question to the minister, the Chair ruled it out of order, stating that it was an important but not very urgent matter.
I should like to take this opportunity to make a few remarks to the minister regarding the livestock feed agency.

February 24, 19G6
Supply-Forestry
I have already expressed my views with regard to this livestock feed agency as well as about the way it could be constituted to best serve the farmers of eastern Canada and those of British Columbia if the latter are included.
Mr. Chairman, I asked the representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and I am also asking the hon. minister, if such a board or agency could secure feed directly from the Canadian Wheat Board or if it would have to go through the usual channels and buy them through wholesalers or brokers who belong to the grain exchange.
I do not see any use in creating such an agency to buy feed grain for the farmers, if it means going through the same channels that exist at the present time, and for the simple reason that it becomes an agency within an agency, which will solve nothing. Somebody else will reap the profits, but that is no solution.
It should be remembered that the Canadian Wheat Board was created in Western Canada, because of the corrupt practices of some brokers who made terrific profits, who wielded tremendous power, whether the crop was good or not. They had absolute control, wheat was bought at prices they indicated, until the farmers put such pressure on the government that it had to establish, in the general interest, the Canadian Wheat Board.
So those brokers were simply pushed back to the boundary or to the lakehead. On the other hand, the Board is now buying wheat from the farmers; its responsibility consists in finding outlets on the foreign market. One thing that intrigues me though is that the board does not resell directly on foreign markets.
I should like to say something about the feed grain agency. We may have to enact special legislation, enabling the agency to negotiate directly with the Canadian Wheat Board as regards direct purchasing, so as to prevent possible intermediates.
Mr. Chairman, at this stage, I am opening a parenthesis to say that we know how much western farmers received when they sold their wheat or when the board sold wheat to Russia, but we do not know how much the Russians paid for it per bushel, which is a different story. We know nothing about the price paid by Russia.
Why? Because brokers acted as go-betweens. As agents, it is necessarily their duty

to negotiate those contracts on foreign markets and to look after the export of the grain.
In any event, we want the feed grain agency to negotiate directly with the Canadian Wheat Board so that the grain many be bought at the best possible price. Besides, the purpose of the Canadian Wheat Board is to see that western farmers do get a fair price for their grain.
However, it is also the responsibility of that agency to negotiate so that eastern farmers get full value in grain supplies and to see that they do not pay exorbitant prices, in brief that the transaction does not result in some speculation between western producers and eastern buyers.
I am therefore asking the minister what will be the exact duties and powers of this feed grain agency or board.
I see an amount of $19.5 million under item 10, so something must have been done in that connection; $705,000 have been paid out in salaries, so someone must have been paid. There has also been publicity; $66,000 were paid out for professional and special services, so something must have been done there too.

Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, February 17, during
DEBATES	1767
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the question period, I put the following question to the hon. Minister of Finance:
In view of the fact that no provision was made for this in the estimates, could the Minister tell the house whether he is considering the necessity of increasing family allowances, and will he inform us of his decision in his next budget?
Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate receiving tonight an answer from the Minister, after I have made the following comments for his information.
The estimates for the 1966-67 fiscal year were tabled recently by the Minister, and they do not indicate an early change in the family allowances pattern.
I understand that the minister has more than one string to his bow. He might very well, if he so decides with his other cabinet colleagues, take action in this field and reveal it to us in his forthcoming budget.
I hope this is one of the important and pleasant surprises he is keeping in store for all Canadians. I know that the minister practises the art of secrecy. But he could give us a ray of hope by recognizing the urgency of increasing family alowances.
Here is a social field that should be substantially reviewed. I do not intend to discuss tonight the question of which government has such a responsibility. I shall deal with this matter when the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare are considered.
I want briefly to demonstrate the necessity of an immediate increase in such allowances.
First, let us say that many provinces and citizens demand that allowances be geared to present needs. At the last meeting of Health and Welfare ministers in Ottawa, in January last, at least five provinces recognized that the family allowances program had to be changed. They are Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
The representative of Quebec, at this conference Mr. Rene Levesque, went so far as to say that if Ottawa failed to act, in view of the urgency of the problem, Quebec would shortly proceed to correct the current inadequacy of the family allowances.
No grudge should be held against provinces that take initiatives because of the inertia and apathy of the federal government.
Several members in this house as well as other Canadians say that the central government should be strong and powerful. Let the central government wake up. Let it take
February 24, 1966
1768	COMMONS DEBATES
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion action. Otherwise dynamic provinces are justified in intervening and in going ahead with their projects.
Indeed, I doubt that the responsibility for family allowances constitutionally falls to Ottawa. The fact that Ottawa intervened in that field in 1944 does not mean that it had the right to do so. But let us set aside the legal aspect today. I shall return to it on another occasion.
I maintain that unless the government takes immediate action, unless it assumes all the responsibility and power which it claims, it will have to allow those provinces that wish to do so to deal with the urgent needs of Canadian families.
Within a few weeks, through his actions or inaction, the minister will be able to give a certain orientation to the improvement of family allowances.
I would surely like to have the minister's views on such a matter which has become urgent mainly because of increased family needs, the rise in the cost of living and the loss in value of our dollar since 1945.
In closing, I should like to remind the minister that between 1945 and 1965 the cost of living increased by 87.7 per cent, while family allowances have only been raised 9.4 per cent. Now is the time, more than ever, to fill the gap.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for 22 years now Canada has operated a family allowance program for mothers and for all children up to the age of 16, provided the children are attending school. More recently, a special youth allowance was introduced for school children aged 16 and 17. The rates are $6, $8 and $10 per month, according to the age of the children. This program has undergone only minor changes in its period of existence of 22 years.
At the last meeting of provincial ministers of welfare with myself in Ottawa, considerable attention was directed to this program of family allowances. It was suggested, especially by the minister from the province of Quebec, that there existed a need for a very careful consideration of the rates of allowance and the children to whom the allowance ought to be paid. In making that suggestion, the minister was re-echoing comments which emanated from other responsible persons,

especially students who have written extensively on this particular subject.
I was able to tell the conference something which I repeated later in the house, namely that the Department of National Health and Welfare is giving very careful study to this question of family allowances. It is a major program affecting the pattern of income of many hundreds of thousands of families and affecting their family budget, as well as assisting millions of children in the country. Any changes ought to be taken only after very careful consideration. Perhaps it is a fact that the amounts paid to each child need revision; perhaps the weighting by age or number of children needs altering and needs up-dating.
It should be borne in mind that these questions, and the determination of any changes in the family allowance program, must be considered in relation to the total social and economic policies of the government, the requirements for assistance of other groups in the community, including the older people and including the requirements of education.

The question which he posed is somewhat more restricted than the content of his speech, with which I am in complete and total accord. The question yesterday was this: Will the minister inform the house whether the National Capital Commission intends to promote the capital across the nation? If so, how and how soon?
The National Capital Commission is an agency established to make plans and assist in the development of the national capital region to make it a suitable place as a capital. This is a continuing job which has been carried on for over 60 years by this commission and its predecessors, since about 1897. Improvement and development of the capital is its main purpose. It can do certain other things only incidental to this main purpose. One of these incidental activities is informing the people of Canada about what it is doing to improve the capital. I believe it is that type of information service which the hon. member spoke about in the early part of his remarks.

subsubtopic: ATLANTIC DEVELOPMENT BOARD-INQUIRY AS TO ADDITIONAL ASSISTANCE TO MARITIMES
speechtext:
On the only other occasion when I used this procedural device to bring a question before the house, fairly good results were obtained. Hon. members may recall that I referred to the closing of McAvity's industrial plant in Saint John, and it was possible to avert this move.
The question I raise tonight has in it some of the same elements-loss of industry, loss of employment and an uninterested provincial government. I see a smiling Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) in his place at this late hour. He is relaxed and confident, now that his own estimates have gone through and he has really nothing to worry about now for the balance of the session.
I hope the minister can help me this evening. This question concerns the exclusion of Saint John, Fredericton, Dartmouth and Halifax from the Area Development Incentives Act. It goes back to 1963 under the old act when certain cities in the maritimes were
February 24, 1966	COMMONS
excluded. Hope was held out that when the new act was introduced in 1965 the situation would be changed. But they were again excluded. My objection is that the mayors and others above been kept on a string; they have been hoodwinked into thinking there was some hope for them under the act. This is not the fault of the Minister of Transport. But it appears, now, that the answer will be a definite "no" and that there will not be an opportunity for the inclusion of the cities I have mentioned in the designated area plan.
We are now faced with the necessity of doing something for these cities in an equivalent way. Everyone knows that they are faced with unique problems in this regard. It appears that the Atlantic Development Board is being considered as one means of assisting them, but this has not been definitely stated.
I think there is need for haste and that immediate efforts should be made to settle this problem.
Its effects have already been shown. Established industries in some of these cities are moving outside the perimeter of the excluded area. Saint John has already lost old established industries which have moved outside to nearby towns, in each case obtaining the grant which is available under the act. In the second place I understand, although I cannot prove this, that there are many industries which wanted to go to larger cities such as Halifax and Saint John-towns which have a labour surplus-but they have not even gone to the maritimes because those towns were not available to them under the terms of the act.
I suggest that the minister, as the minister responsible for the Atlantic Development Board, should direct the board to take this matter under advisement if it has not already done so. The board should be asked to look into it immediately, call for briefs if necessary from the cities and get right down to business. It is not the hon. gentleman's fault. The government could have avoided this situation by bringing these cities in earlier without any trouble. They have been playing around with the industrial future of these cities.
I think it is high time we had an answer to this question. If the minister wants an example of a method by which an equivalent amount could be given I suggest he take an amount of money and have it administered initially by the board. If necessary it could be channeled through the two agencies in New

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Brunswick and Nova Scotia, Industrial Estates in Nova Scotia and the Productivity Council in New Brunswick, and let them deal with this matter, or at least be a party to advising where assistance can be given. I hope the minister will not think that some of the other benefits, some very good benefits, that are given to these particular cities- wharves, roads, harbour bridges-are part of it. There must be a fully equivalent benefit to the cities that have been forgotten and stalled by this government.
